title: OpenFOAM Extensions
text:
1 OpenFOAM Extensions
Curated OpenFOAM 13 directory with additional workflow tools.

title: OpenFOAM Extensions
text:
1.1 Prerequisites
This respository aims at being homogeneous in the sense it tries to keep a consistent toolset across all cases. Shell automation is done solely with bash and indirectly through Python in some cases. Unless otherwise specified, the following tools are used:

OpenFOAM v13
Python managed by uv
Quarto with Typst support
Apptainer with Docker/Podman

title: OpenFOAM Extensions
text:
1.2 Before starting
Many features available in this repository rely on the environment configuration provided by etc/bashrc. In general the scripts will source that file for you, but environment configuration will not remain in CLI after the script finishes. To experience a smooth experience, it is recommended to source that file in your current shell from this directory:
source $PWD/etc/bashrc
If you want this to be done automatically for every new bash session, you can append that to your ~/.bashrc by calling foam_source_append. This function only appends the configuration if not already present and tests for the existence of the configuration file so that your shell will not raise error messages if you delete this repository later.

title: OpenFOAM Extensions
text:
1.3 Compilation methods
It is possible to build the whole extensions library or isolated features, depending on your needs. The following logic is applied throughout this sources directory:

If a directory provides an Allwmake file, it allows to compile the whole tree below it; this is the case for the root directory, for instance.
If a directory of src/ provides a subdirectory called Make/, then it supports the individual library build which is done by running wmake libso from that directory.

All builds are written to $FOAM_USER_APPBIN and $FOAM_USER_LIBBIN.
The simplest way it to build everything from the repository root:
./Allwmake

If you encounter failures when loading a library, please consider running ./Allwclean first to clear the build cache. Sometimes previous build artifacts may cause unexpected behavior.

title: OpenFOAM Extensions
text:
1.4 Running tests
Some libraries may provide test programs under a test/ sub-directory, and all of them are structured in the same way. The following instructions indicate how to build, run, and clean those directories.
To build and run the test suite:
cd test
./Allrun
To clean test build artifacts:
cd test
./Allclean

title: OpenFOAM Extensions
text:
1.5 Running cases
Whenever possible, cases are meant to be run from within an Apptainer instance. The SIF file can be generated from the root of this repository by running make image It can be later transferred to any HPC environment where Apptainer is supported, ensuring a consisten environment. Assuming you are connected to the target compute node, the following elements indicate how to instantiate an environment, run the simulation, and inspect partial results on demand. Notice that we will make use of the screen utility to keep services alive even if one disconnects from the node.

Connecting to a session:

# Declare variables to set the case to be run:
APP_NAME="methaneAirSensitivity"
APP_PATH="tutorials/multicomponentFluid/$APP_NAME"

# A SIF generated by `make image` should be named like this:
SIF_FILE="${name}-$(whoami).sif"

# Start a named screen session:
screen -S $APP_NAME

# Start apptainer instance on the background:
apptainer instance start -B $PWD --writable-tmpfs $SIF_FILE $APP_NAME

# Enter running instance in shell mode:
apptainer shell instance://$APP_NAME

From within a session, setup the base environment and run the case(s):

# Instantiate the environment from instance:
(cd $APP_PATH && uv sync)

# Move into the simulation directory and run:
(cd $APP_PATH && ./Allrun &)

# Ctrl + A, D to detach screen

Inspecting a running simulation (from the same node as above):

# Attach to the running screen session
screen -r $APP_NAME

# Enter running instance in shell mode:
apptainer shell instance://$APP_NAME

# Move into the simulation directory and check status:
cd $APP_PATH

# Start Jupyter server to connect from case notebook:
uv run jupyter-notebook --no-browser --ip=0.0.0.0 \
    --ServerApp.token='' --ServerApp.password=''

Stop instance after working:

# Stop instance after working:
apptainer instance stop $APP_NAME

title: 2  Contributing
text: 2.1 Directives

title: 2  Contributing
text:
Comments added by this repository to explain changes performed to base libraries are tagged with // WWW: so that they can be tracked in the future.
Whenever possible/applicable, copy the original files list from the library you are modifying to use as a starting point. Remove or comment out files that are not implemented in this repository. Modify the base path of LIB to use LIB = $(FOAM_USER_LIBBIN)/<your-library-name> so that the path is writable.
The same apply to options, which requires a few extra guidelines concerning its declared variables:

EXE_INC: keep the original list untouched, add the local include directories in the end. Sometimes the library will fail to compile because the original list was lacking something (in a library as OpenFOAM it probably worked because the missing files were sourced elsewhere during compilation and the authors never had to add then), append these in the end so that we can distinguish them from the ones already in the list.
LIB_LIBS: it the project compiles but on run-time there is a missing linking library, but proceed as for EXE_INC by listing the library in the end. It might be tricky to identify where the functionality comes from, maybe start by ls $FOAM_LIBBIN and look for possibly related files.

A Makefile is provided in the root directory: running make will generate a local documentation, make publish can be used by admins to publish to GitHub Pages, and make clean strips the generated outputs and intermediate files from the folder.

title: 3  Changelog
text:
Added an exhaustive, readable, and well-commented test suite in etc/test.sh covering all shell functions under etc/rc/ (utilsrc, coresrc, meshingrc) with strict 80-character line wrapping, deterministic mocking, and comprehensive edge-case assertions.
Enhanced safe_run_ncores in etc/rc/coresrc to accept an arbitrary sequence of fallback core counts. If the primary requested core count exceeds physical cores, fallback values are evaluated in order; if none are feasible or provided, execution falls back to half of the available physical cores. Also changed display of messages by sourcin utilsrc from corerc and improved re-sourcing time by testing for WM_PROJECT in bashrc.

title: 3  Changelog
text:
3.2 2026-09-16

Adapted extendedThermoCloud to upcast the solid object to a tabulatedSolid as a prototype for temperature dependent properties. Currently this supports a single species and need to be generalized in the future.
Unified the build of all libraries under a single Allwmake at the sources root, following the full library standard. Added compilation instructions at multiple levels to README.md
Added extendedThermoCloud support by extending thermoCloud; this extension if fact only needed working with thermoParcel as the physics was found to be at the parcel level. Added related library sources under lagrangian/parcel/{cloud,parcels}.

title: 4  jmakLaplacianFoam
text:
Solver for time-temperature reactive heat release in solids. Implements differential Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) reaction progress kinetics for non-isothermal process as proposed by Mittemeijer et al..
In the future, it would be desirable to have the following features implemented:

Handle non-linearities in thermal properties.
Generalization for an arbitrary number of reactions.
Implement solidThermo to use externalWallHeatFluxTemperature.


This solver was initially implemented and tested with OpenFOAM v2212 and later migrated to OpenFOAM 13. The original implementation is made available under legacy directory and is no longer maintained.

title: 5  Lagrangian
text:
5.1.1 Extended Thermo Parcel

Provides a variant of thermoCloud with varying specific heat.

Important: this extension currently support a single solid phase which needs to be a tabulatedSolid as provided in the thermophysical properties below. This will need to be generalized at some point.
Extending a parcel requires several templates to be adapted. The following building blocks are present in the implementation of extendedThermoCloud:

Parcel template class in found in ExtendedThermoParcel
The derived parcel instantiation extendedThermoParcel
The derived cloud instantiation extendedThermoCloud

Or in a tree view:
parcel
├── clouds
│   └── derived
│       └── extendedThermoCloud
│           ├── extendedThermoCloud.C
│           └── extendedThermoCloud.H
└── parcels
    ├── Templates
    │   └── ExtendedThermoParcel
    │       ├── ExtendedThermoParcel.C
    │       ├── ExtendedThermoParcel.H
    │       ├── ExtendedThermoParcelI.H
    │       ├── ExtendedThermoParcelIO.C
    │       ├── ExtendedThermoParcelName.C
    │       └── ExtendedThermoParcelTrackingDataI.H
    └── derived
        └── extendedThermoParcel
            ├── extendedThermoParcel.H
            └── makeExtendedThermoParcelSubmodels.C
For using it, append the following to controlDict (it depends on extended thermophysical properties so that non-constant properties are supported):
libs
(
    "libextendedThermophysicalProperties.so"
    "libextendedLagrangianParcel.so"
);

7  JMAK Solid Kinetics
text:
NoteAbout



Sample case can be found here. It illustrates the use of jmakLaplacianFoam solver provided in this repository.


Simulate the temperature evolution of a reacting cylinder (diameter 3 inches and height of 6 inches) immersed in coded external convective boundary conditions representing steady air at room temperature. The solid is undergoing volumetric reactions represented by a JMAK kinetics with heat release, leading to a thermal build-up near the sample core. This could represent, e.g., a cement hydration process.
Figure 7.1 illustrates the temperature evolution at a probe placed near the core of the cylinder. The humps are associated to the different reactions that take place over time.








Figure 7.1: Thermal history at probe location.





Figure 7.2 demonstrates how the temperature is distributed in a vertical cut of the cylinder after 8h. Plots of beta indicate the JMAK progress of the reaction: we see that reaction 1 has saturated at 1.23, enabling reaction 2 that has already progressed considerably, and reaction 3 is still in earlier stage.








Figure 7.2: Temperature profile at a slice of the domain after 8h.

title: 8  Silica Particle Melting
text:
NoteAbout



Sample case can be found here. It intends to illustrate the proper capture of a solid particle melting, as supported by the following libraries provided in this repository:

libextendedThermophysicalProperties: provides tabulatedSolid, used for representation of piecewise-linear silica properties, allowing the incorporation of the lumped reaction enthalpies in specific heat.
libextendedLagrangianParcel: provides extendedThermoCloud allowing the simulation of non-constant properties lagrangian particles.



Simulates the heating of a single silica particle immersed in the flue gases from propane-oxygen combustion. Fluid properties were processed with Cantera and fit to polynomials to match the temperature dependence of adiabatic combustion flue gases (equilibrium computed under constant enthalpy and pressure). Solid specific heat capacity was modified to include smeared latent heat of phase transitions where applicable.
Figure 8.1 displays the thermal history of a single particle under the above conditions. Phase changes produce flat regions, notably the large plateau observed in between \(23-32\text{ms}\) associated to the melting of the particle, thus representing the intended goal of capturing the expected silica latent heat of fusion. Since the domain has been intentionally oversized with respect to the required energy to melt the particle, we observe a temperature increase beyond melting point, as expected.








Figure 8.1: Verification of single particle heating thermal history.











NoteTo-do




Simulate the same case with the base thermoCloud to illustrate the uncontrolled heating the particle would undergo without latent heat incorporation.

title: 9  Tutorials
text:
9.1 General
Unlike the sample cases, which are intended to be minimal working examples of the extensions provided here, the tutorials are full fledged case studies that may or may not include the extensions provided here. These illustrate the authors main skills and document complex workflows that go beyond the scope of tutorials provided with OpenFOAM.

9.2 multicomponentFluid

methaneAirSensitivity: illustrates the simulation of methane combustion in a co-axial burner under different operating conditions. The main goals are to provide a robust setup for combustion simulations.
